title: How to Build Customer Trust When Selling Online in Pakistan
summary: How to build customer trust when selling online in Pakistan: cash on delivery, honest photos, published numbers, confirmation calls and a return policy.
body_markdown:
Customer trust in Pakistan is not won with a slogan. It is won by removing the buyer's risk before they have to take it. Most people buying from a small online seller here have been burned themselves or heard the story from someone who was: money sent in advance, parcel never arrived, or a product that looked nothing like the photo.


So the seller who gets the order is the one who answers the buyer's real question — *what happens to me if this goes wrong?* — before it is asked. In practice that means five things: take cash on delivery, show the product honestly, be a findable person rather than an anonymous page, state the door price and delivery time in plain numbers, and handle the one order that goes wrong properly.


The rest of this guide is how to do each one, in the order that matters for a new page with no reviews yet.


## Why Pakistani buyers start out suspicious


You are not selling into a neutral market. You are selling after years of the following, and your buyer is pricing all of it into their decision:


- **Advance-payment scams.** Someone asked for an EasyPaisa or JazzCash transfer, then stopped replying. This is the single memory that decides most first orders.
- **The photo-versus-parcel gap.** A stock image from a supplier catalogue, a very different item in the box. Buyers now assume the photo is the best case, not the real case.
- **Pages that disappear.** A Facebook page with no name behind it, no address, no phone number that gets answered — and nowhere to go once the parcel is wrong.
- **No recourse.** Returning something to an individual seller usually means arguing over WhatsApp with a person who has already been paid.
- **Silence.** A question asked at 9pm answered two days later, if at all. Buyers read slow replies as a sign that nobody is really running the shop.


None of this is personal. It is a rational response to a market where the buyer usually pays first and hopes. The useful way to read it: every item on that list is a risk the buyer is being asked to carry, and every trust signal below is you taking one of them back. If you want the seller's-eye view of the same problem,[how to avoid dropshipping scams in Pakistan](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/avoid-dropshipping-scams-pakistan) covers the fraud patterns from the other side of the transaction.


## The trust signals that actually move an order


Not all signals are worth the same. These are in rough order of how much they change a stranger's decision to buy.


### Cash on delivery is the loudest one


COD is not just a payment method in Pakistan. It is the buyer's insurance policy, and offering it moves a first order more than anything else you can put in an ad. The buyer keeps their money until the parcel is in their hand, which means the worst case for them is a few minutes wasted at the door instead of cash gone.


If you sell prepaid-only, you are asking a stranger to take the exact risk the market has taught them not to take. There are sellers who can do that — established brands, people with years of public reviews — but a new page is not one of them. Offer COD first, and add prepaid later as an option for repeat buyers, ideally with a small incentive rather than as the only choice.[COD dropshipping in Pakistan](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/cod-dropshipping-in-pakistan) explains how the collection side of it works if you have never run it.


### Photograph the product you will actually send


Supplier catalogue images are the fastest route to a refused parcel. They are lit professionally, often styled on a different model, and sometimes a different colourway than the unit that ships. The buyer at the door compares the box to the picture in their head, not to your listing.


What to do instead, in rising order of effort:


- **Add one real photo** of the actual item in ordinary daylight, in your hand or on a plain surface. One honest photo next to the catalogue shot beats ten polished ones.
- **Show scale.** Put a familiar object beside it — a phone, a hand, a water bottle. Most size complaints are the buyer's imagination, not your description.
- **Publish measurements, not sizes.** For clothing and shoes, chest, length and sleeve in inches, and the foot length the shoe actually fits. S/M/L means different things to different suppliers.
- **Shoot a ten-second video.** Turn the item over, open the zip, show the stitching. Video is the hardest thing for a fake page to produce, so buyers read it as proof that you hold the item.
- **Name the flaws.** If the fabric is thin or the print is slightly off-centre, say it. Sellers are astonished by how well this converts. It also removes your most expensive returns.


The words matter as much as the pictures. A description that lists the material, the measurements and what the item is not for reads as written by someone who has handled it —[how to write product descriptions that sell](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/how-to-write-product-descriptions-that-sell) goes through the structure.


### Be a person, not an anonymous page


Buyers check whether there is a human behind the shop before they order. Make it easy for them to find one:


- A real name and face on the page, not just a logo.
- A phone number and a WhatsApp that get answered during stated hours.
- A city. Even "based in Lahore, we deliver nationwide" reassures people, because it means you exist somewhere.
- A page that has posted consistently, not one created last week with twelve products and a countdown timer.
- The same business name across the page, the packaging and the message you send. Mismatched names read as a scam even when they are not.


### Put the numbers where the buyer can see them


Every number you hide becomes a doubt, and doubts are answered in the buyer's head with the worst case. Publish all four of these before anyone has to ask:


- **The door price in PKR** — product plus delivery, the total the rider will ask for. A buyer who hears a higher number at the door usually refuses, and they are not wrong to.
- **The delivery time** as a range you can actually keep. Under-promise here; a parcel that beats its estimate creates a repeat customer.
- **The return window and what qualifies.** Even a short, strictly defined window beats no statement at all.
- **Who pays return delivery** in the cases you allow. Vagueness here is what turns a small problem into a public complaint.


## Your reply speed is part of the product


For most small sellers the first message is the whole sale. A stranger has decided to test whether you are real, and how you reply tells them.


Reply fast, in the language the buyer used, with their actual question answered. Urdu question, Urdu answer. If someone asks the price, send the door price rather than "inbox for price" — that phrase costs more sales than it saves. Send a real photo when asked, not the catalogue one again.


Then stop selling. Once you have answered, one clear next step is enough: "Should I place the order for you?" Pressure tactics — fake stock counts, an offer that expires in an hour — work on a small number of buyers and permanently lose the rest, because they are exactly the tactics a scam page uses.


Set hours you can honestly keep and put them on the page. "We reply 10am–10pm" that is true builds more trust than "24/7 support" that is not.


## The confirmation call does two jobs


Calling before dispatch is usually framed as a way to cut returns, and it is one. It is also the moment most of your trust gets built, because it is the first time the buyer hears a human voice attached to the shop.


Keep it short and cover four things: confirm the item and any variant, read back the full address, state the exact cash amount the rider will ask for, and give the delivery window. Then ask if they have a question. That call alone removes the two biggest causes of a refused parcel — an order that was never serious, and a buyer surprised by the amount at the door.


If the buyer sounds hesitant, do not push. Ask what is making them unsure and answer it; you will usually hear the real objection, and it is often something you can fix in the listing for every future buyer. For the measurement side of this,[COD return rates in Pakistan and how to cut yours](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/cod-return-rates-in-pakistan-how-to-reduce-them) shows how to score your own rate and work out what a failed parcel costs you.


## Social proof you can collect honestly


New sellers have no reviews, which feels like a chicken-and-egg problem. It is not — it is a collection problem, and the fix starts with your first delivered order.


- **Ask after delivery, not before.** A message the day after a parcel lands: "Did it reach you okay?" Some of those replies are your first testimonials, and every one of them is a chance to catch a problem before it becomes a complaint.
- **Screenshot real WhatsApp replies** with the buyer's permission, and blur the number. Ordinary, slightly misspelled messages read as true. Polished five-star quotes do not.
- **Post delivery proof.** Parcels packed for dispatch, courier receipts with the details hidden, a photo a customer sent of the item in use.
- **Answer public complaints in public.** A handled complaint on your page is stronger proof than a wall of praise, because it shows a buyer what happens when something goes wrong.
- **Never buy reviews or invent a customer.** Fake proof is recognisable — the same phrasing, no history, all posted in one week — and being caught once destroys the thing you were trying to build.


## The parcel itself is a trust signal


The unboxing is the only physical contact your shop has with the buyer, and it decides whether they order twice. A sealed, undamaged parcel with your business name on it, a slip inside that says what was ordered and how to reach you, and the item packed so it survives a courier van — that is most of it. A loose item in a reused bag with a marker scrawl says the shop is temporary, even when the product is good.


You do not need expensive printing. Consistency matters more than cost.[Packaging and branding for small online sellers in Pakistan](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/packaging-branding-for-small-online-sellers-in-pakistan) covers what a COD parcel actually has to survive and the cheapest ways to make yours look deliberate.


## What you do when an order goes wrong


Some parcels will arrive damaged, late, or wrong. This is not the failure — how you handle it is, and it is also the biggest trust opportunity you get. A buyer whose problem was fixed quickly tells more people than a buyer whose order was simply fine.


- **Reply the same day** , even if the fix takes longer. Silence is what turns a complaint into a public post.
- **Ask for a photo** , then decide. Do not argue about whose fault it was in the first message.
- **Fix it in one step where you can** — a replacement or a refund under your stated policy, without making the buyer ask three times.
- **Say what you will do and by when** , then do that. A missed promise costs more than the original problem.
- **Log the reason.** If two buyers report the same fault, the product or the listing is the problem, not the buyers.


Write your policy down before you need it, in one short paragraph, and apply it the same way every time. Deciding case by case under pressure is how sellers end up with inconsistent stories that customers screenshot and compare.

## A trust checklist before your next ad


Run this list over the page you are about to spend money sending people to:


- Is cash on delivery offered and stated clearly?
- Is there at least one photo of the real item, not only catalogue images?
- Are measurements published for anything size-dependent?
- Is the door price in PKR, including delivery, visible without asking?
- Is the delivery time stated as a range you can keep?
- Is the return policy written down in one short paragraph?
- Is there a real name, a city and a number that gets answered?
- Is there any proof — one screenshot, one delivery photo, one customer message?
- Do you confirm every order by call before dispatch?
- Do you know what you will do the next time a parcel arrives damaged?


Ten boxes. Most new sellers can tick four. Fixing the other six costs nothing but an afternoon, and it changes the return on every rupee of ad spend that follows. Browse[the Markaz categories](https://www.markaz.app/shop/categories) when you are ready to pick what to list next.


## Frequently asked questions


### How do I build trust as a brand new seller with no reviews?


Take cash on delivery, post one real photo or short video of the actual item, put a name and an answered phone number on the page, and state the door price and delivery time openly. Those four cost nothing and cover the exact risks buyers are worried about. Then collect proof from your first deliveries and post it.


### Is cash on delivery necessary in Pakistan?


For a new seller, close to it. COD lets a buyer keep their money until the parcel is in their hands, which answers the advance-payment fear that decides most first orders. Established brands with public review histories can sell prepaid; a page with no history generally cannot.


### How do I get reviews when I have no customers yet?


Message every buyer the day after delivery and ask whether the parcel arrived fine. Save the replies, ask permission to share them, and blur the numbers. Ordinary messages read as genuine. Never invent a customer or buy reviews — being caught once undoes everything.


### Should I show the price publicly or ask people to message?


Show it. "Inbox for price" reads as either hiding something or quoting different people differently, and most buyers scroll past rather than ask. Publish the door price including delivery, so the amount the rider asks for is the amount the buyer already agreed to.


### What should my return policy say?


One short paragraph: what window you accept returns in, what condition the item must be in, which reasons qualify, and who pays return delivery in each case. A modest policy that you apply consistently earns more trust than a generous one you argue about.


### Does selling through a platform help with trust?


It covers the parts you cannot cover yourself. Selling on a platform such as Markaz means cash on delivery collection, the courier leg and a return window with buyer protection are handled under a stated policy, so the buyer is not relying only on your word. Your listings, your replies and your confirmation call still decide whether the order is placed.
